Retain the author's description as quasi-experimental in the narrative, but this is not non-random allocation under the codebook. There is one class per arm.

Criterion 2: 81 students analyzed (42 + 39). Criterion 3: the only creativity measure is a self-report scale; the instructor-rated project score is a quality rubric (instruction, science, technology, artistry, operability) on a PowerPoint courseware task, and the paper does not say whether the AI teacher was available while the post-test project was made."}
corrections.source_says: Under the codebook, set criterion_1_random_assignment_of_ai = met, criterion_3_outcome_scored_on_output = met, core = yes, and context_class = none; retain criterion_2_at_least_50_people = met. Route to the two-screener pipeline. The qualifying output is the instructor-rated quality/usefulness of students' multimedia courseware designs, consistent with the existing usefulness construct; it is not the self-reported Creative Thinking Tendency Scale. The rubric assesses instructional suitability, content correctness, materials, artistry and interface usability. It does not provide a novelty or diversity score. Figure 2 also permits creation of new works. Class-level assignment and unknown AI availability at the post-test must remain explicit.
corrections.quote: The scoring rubric consisted of five dimensions: instruction, science, technology, artistry and operability. Its perfect score was 100, as shown in Table 1.
corrections.locator: PDF p. 6 (journal p. 45), courseware task and Figure 2; PDF p. 9 (journal p. 48), Participants; PDF p. 10 (journal p. 49), Data collection instruments and Table 1; codebook sections 1, 3 and 6.

corrections.source_says: Specify that each student's project score averages two experienced instructors' ratings on a 100-point rubric covering instruction, science, technology, artistry and operability. The reported analysis uses the resulting student-level scores, not individual rater observations. This is an output-quality/usefulness composite, not a direct rating of novelty or overall creativity.

confirmed: The entire markdown conversion was read through the final reference and publication notice; there is no appended supplement. The local PDF has 19 pages and is the 2023 journal article by Hai-Feng Li in Australasian Journal of Educational Technology 39(5), 40-58; source.version and the journal-to-PDF page mapping are correct (PDF pp. 1 and 19; journal pp. 40 and 58).

There is one comparative classroom experiment. The development-stage interviews and end-of-study interviews do not supply additional randomized creativity experiments (PDF p. 5, journal p. 44, Instructional design model; PDF pp. 9-13, journal pp. 48-52, experiment and results).

The analyzed sample is 81 people, with 42 experimental and 39 control students; it is not a count of projects or ratings and is not below 50. The reported average age is 20 (PDF p. 9, journal p. 48, Participants; PDF p. 11, Table 2; PDF p. 13, Table 8).

The same teacher instructed both groups. Common instruction lasted three weeks, the pre-test occurred in the fourth week, ChatGPT-FLGA/T-FLGA lasted three weeks, and the narrative places the post-test in the eighth week (PDF p. 9, journal p. 48, Participants and Experimental procedure).

The AI teacher used ChatGPT through Tencent QQ and a local server, supplied daily learning tasks, and answered students during pre-class and in-class activities. A specific ChatGPT model version is not stated (PDF pp. 5-6, journal pp. 44-45, ChatGPT-FLGA and the learning system).

S1-O1 reported statistics all match: experimental N = 42, mean 88.80, SD 2.73, adjusted mean 89.93, SE 0.43; control N = 39, mean 87.27, SD 3.41, adjusted mean 87.13, SE 0.45; F = 8.32, partial eta squared = 0.09. Table 2 marks p < 0.05 and its accompanying prose prints p = 0.00 < 0.05 (PDF p. 11, journal p. 50).

S1-O2 reported statistics all match: experimental N = 42, mean 19.19, SD 3.00, adjusted mean 19.07, SE 0.44; control N = 39, mean 17.28, SD 3.96, adjusted mean 17.40, SE 0.46; F = 6.85, partial eta squared = 0.08. Table 8 marks p < 0.05 and its accompanying prose prints p = 0.01 < 0.05 (PDF p. 13, journal p. 52).

Creative thinking tendency is a five-item, five-point Likert self-report scale adapted from Lai and Hwang (2014), not creativity scored on produced work. Its name, self_report measure, scored_on_output = false and question = none are correct (PDF p. 10, journal p. 49, Data collection instruments).

The one_line_finding accurately labels project performance versus self-reported creative thinking tendency and reproduces the adjusted means and test results printed in Tables 2 and 8 (PDF pp. 11 and 13, journal pp. 50 and 52).

The experiment reports a one-way ANCOVA controlling pre-project scores or pre-questionnaire ratings. With one class per arm, its reported student-level ANCOVA is not described as accounting for class-level assignment; 81 analyzed students are not 81 independent randomization units (PDF p. 9, Participants; PDF p. 11, Experimental results).

This is not a synthesis and supplies no pooled estimates or diversity outcome; the synthesis defaults are appropriate. No preregistration, supplementary material, shared-sample claim, or public data/code link is stated in the complete document (PDF pp. 1-19; instruments and outcome tables on PDF pp. 10-13).
No company involvement is reported; the stated funding is from the Ministry of Education, China, grant DCA180324 (PDF p. 15, journal p. 54, Acknowledgements).
summary: The paper reports class-level random assignment of 81 students and instructor-rated quality of multimedia courseware designs, so it belongs in the two-screener pipeline under the codebook's usefulness criterion. All reported result numbers and the one-line finding match the PDF; corrections address classification, allocation counts, sample description, incomplete fields, and unconfirmed AI availability at post-test.
